newsitem.title: GERMANY: Punish Kohl, German opposition tells Hesse voters.
newsitem.headline: Punish Kohl, German opposition tells Hesse voters.

text.p: Germany's opposition parties, keen to exploit a general mood of uncertainty, have exhorted voters to punish Chancellor Helmut Kohl in local elections on Sunday for presiding over the worst unemployment since Adolf Hitler's rise to power.

Heavyweights from all parties, including Kohl, have descended on the state of Hesse in recent weeks well aware that elections to local councils here are the main test of voter reaction this year to Germany's economic problems.

"Turn the local election into a settling of accounts for the unfair policies of Kohl's government," Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), told a party gathering in Hesse's capital, Wiesbaden, this week.
Some 4.5 million people are eligible to vote in Hesse and 180,000 citizens from other European Union countries living in the state will be allowed to vote for the first time.
The voting will also include an election to the city parliament for Frankfurt, Germany's banking capital.

While opinion pollsters believe the vote will at best give a distorted picture of political sentiment in Germany, analysts say political leaders have given the elections such prominence that they are bound to have a nationwide relevance.
"Politicians have pushed this and raised expectations so much that they will have to let themselves be measured by the outcome," said Thomas Mayer, an analyst at Goldman Sachs.
"One will look at who are the winners and losers and then take nationwide political conclusions. I'm pretty sure financial markets will look at this."

After decades of relative wealth and prosperity Germans today find themselves constantly confronted with unemployment and welfare cutbacks as Kohl strives to get Germany's finances in shape for his pet project -- European monetary union.
Joblessness in January jumped more than half a million people to 4.66 million and Kohl's government has come under heavy fire for failing to deal with the problem.

The dual evils of inflation and unemployment were the death of Germany's early experiment in democracy in the 1920s and continue to haunt politicians in the stable democratic state that has arisen since World War Two.

One leading pollster said this week that Germans were losing confidence in their future and now see themselves as living through upheaval and uncertainty in the years following the absorbtion of the formerly communist east.
"After a month in which unemployment rose by 500,000, Kohl is breaking into a sweat," Greens leader Joschka Fischer told a campaign meeting in Frankfurt this week.

A poll published last Friday showed Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU), its Bavarian sister party CSU and the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) would have lost their majority in the Bundestag or lower house of the federal parliament if a general election had been held last weekend.
But recent polls show that despite Kohl's problems at the national level, his CDU will gain in the election to Frankfurt's parliament on Sunday while the SPD will emerge as clear losers.

A poll by the Mannheim-based Ipos institute published last Sunday put CDU support in Frankfurt at 37 percent, up from 33.4 percent in the last local election in 1993, due mainly to the popularity of the city's CDU mayor Petra Roth.
The SPD is shown falling to 28 percent from 32 percent while the Greens are the biggest gainers, rising to 19 percent from 14 percent.

The FDP, led in Frankfurt by German Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis, are expected to enter Frankfurt's town hall for the first time in 16 years with a vote of six percent, up from 4.4 percent in 1993 which was below the minimum of five percent required to take office.

The far right Republicans are expected to lose ground but will remain in parliament with six percent of the vote, down from 9.3 percent last time. The mainstream parties have said they would not enter a coalition with the Republicans.
It was unclear, however, whether the CDU would obtain the votes needed to stake a claim in government in Frankfurt.

In Hesse overall, the SPD was the strongest party in the last local elections in 1993 with a 36.4 percent share of the vote, followed by the CDU with 32.0 percent, the Greens with 11.0 percent and the FDP with 5.1 percent.
